AMD Is Down 26% and Intel Is Down 42%. Which AI Stock Is Worth Buying on the Dip?
RJ Fulton, The Motley Fool

INTC
OPAI.PVT

The recent semiconductor sell-off has presented investors with potentially attractive buying opportunities as concerns surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) valuations weigh on the sector. Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) have fallen approximately 26% and 42% from their respective recent highs.

AMD has established itself as a major supplier of high-performance computing products, capitalizing on growing demand for AI infrastructure. Intel, meanwhile, is pursuing an ambitious turnaround centered on restoring its competitive position in processor design and semiconductor manufacturing.

While both companies stand to benefit from continued investment in AI, their contrasting financial performance, capital requirements, and competitive positions present two distinct investment opportunities.

The case for Advanced Micro Devices

AMD designs high-performance processors and accelerators for data centers, personal computers, and gaming systems. Its expanding portfolio of AI accelerators and multiyear strategic partnership with OpenAI position the company to capture a greater share of AI infrastructure spending. Meanwhile, established relationships with companies such as Sony and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) provide additional revenue streams through its gaming business.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached approximately $45.4 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 41.9%. AMD generated $7.6 billion in net income over the same period, translating to a profit margin of roughly 16.8%. Its ability to deliver substantial revenue growth while maintaining profitability is particularly attractive as investors increasingly scrutinize the financial performance of AI-related companies.

As of December 2025, AMD maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.1 and a current ratio of 2.9, reflecting a relatively strong balance sheet. The company also generated approximately $6.7 billion in free cash flow during fiscal 2025, although stock-based compensation accounted for 21.2% of operating cash flow.

The case for Intel

Intel designs and manufactures processors for personal computers, data centers, and networking applications. While its established processor business remains a significant source of revenue, much of Intel's long-term investment thesis centers on its foundry strategy. By expanding its semiconductor manufacturing capabilities, Intel aims to compete for manufacturing contracts from other chip designers while reducing its reliance on traditional processor sales.

title: Jensen Huang's exit is part of a troubling CEO scandal history
detail:
Jensen Huang's exit is part of a troubling CEO scandal history
Damilola Esebame
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 1:13 PM MST 5 min read
NVDA
INTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Jensen Huang spent 33 years building Nvidia into the company at the center of the artificial intelligence industry, but his departure unfolded within days. 

The board accepted his resignation on Nov. 11, 2026, following allegations of personal conduct and foreign intelligence concerns that prompted an independent investigation, according to Nvidia's 8-K filing. 

Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress became interim Chief Executive Officer (CEO), while Harvey C. Jones took over as board chair.

The leadership shake-up came as Nvidia was already shedding roughly $1.59 trillion in shareholder wealth, with shares down about 30% from their recent high, Axios reported.

Huang's departure also highlights a wider pattern, with six other publicly traded companies losing their top executives over controversies since 2018.

Also Read: Jensen Huang sends bold message to Nvidia shareholders

Intel's Krzanich set the semiconductor precedent for Nvidia

Nvidia's leadership crisis has a close historical parallel at Intel, where a similar controversy forced the semiconductor giant to replace its chief executive eight years earlier.

Intel's Brian Krzanich resigned in June 2018 after the company confirmed his consensual relationship with an employee violated its workplace relationship policy.

Krzanich had led Intel since 2013 and joined the company as an engineer in 1982, making his departure a significant leadership change. His resignation left Intel searching for a permanent replacement, while Chief Financial Officer Robert Swan stepped in as interim chief executive.

Both Krzanich and Huang led major semiconductor companies when personal conduct issues threatened their leadership, and neither company had a designated successor ready.

In both situations, the boards responded quickly by turning to their chief financial officers to provide temporary leadership during the transition.

Intel's shares initially remained relatively stable after Krzanich resigned, but the company later struggled to maintain its competitive position against rivals.

Nvidia now faces a similar leadership challenge, with no publicly identified successor and an important earnings report approaching just days after Huang's departure.

From Nestlé to BP, five more leaders fell to conduct and disclosure failures

Nestlé dismissed Laurent Freixe as CEO in September 2025 after finding his undisclosed relationship with a direct subordinate violated its code of conduct. 

Freixe received no exit package after exactly one year as CEO, making his ouster the second time in 12 months that the Swiss food giant lost its top leader, Reuters reported.

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Qualcomm's free cash flow over the past twelve months equals 5.0% of its market value, compared with 4.4% for the median S&P 500 company. That cash belongs to shareholders whether or not it is paid out, and share prices tend to follow cash that keeps coming. A yield above the median marks either a business on sale or one the market expects to shrink. So why is the market paying less for Qualcomm's cash than for the median company's?

Qualcomm's Free Cash Flow Fell By A Third

The price appears to assume that Qualcomm's cash will keep shrinking, and over the past year it has. Free cash flow came to $8.65 billion in the twelve months to September 27, 2026, down from $12.8 billion a year earlier. That fall came after two years of gains, from $9.85 billion in fiscal 2023 to $11.2 billion in fiscal 2024 and $12.8 billion in fiscal 2025.

Qualcomm's free cash flow fell by a third in a single year. If Qualcomm is a large share of your savings, another year like that could mean a fall you would have to sit through. Selling instead could bring a heavy tax bill. Our partner advisory firm will take your question on a free 30-minute call, by phone or video, with no obligation. Book a free call.

Qualcomm (QCOM) sells chips for phones, cars and other devices, and it licenses its patents to phone makers. The business requires little capital. Capital spending consumed only 22.4% of operating cash over the past twelve months, leaving free cash flow equal to 20.1% of revenue.

Profitability has slipped alongside the cash. The operating margin was 20.1% over the past twelve months, compared with 28.0% a year earlier and 25.8% two years earlier. Qualcomm also owes $15.1 billion, against $7.68 billion in cash and short-term investments. So far, the figures lean toward a shrinking business rather than one on sale.

Qualcomm Loses Apple Chip Sales As Phone Market Shrinks

On its November 4, 2026 call, management said Qualcomm is losing Apple as a buyer of its phone chips. It also said the mobile industry has shrunk because of memory pricing. Revenue fell 8.4% in fiscal Q4 2026 from a year earlier. The company expects phone chip revenue in fiscal Q1 2027 to fall by a mid single digit percentage from the quarter before. Sales of chips for Apple products are winding down.

Qualcomm's answer is data center chips. The company targets $5 billion of data center revenue in fiscal 2027, mostly from custom chips built for two large cloud customers. That target would equal about 12% of the $43.1 billion in revenue Qualcomm reported over the past twelve months. It is a forecast, however, not a result. The licensing business looks steadier. Management says licensing revenue is running at the same pace as before, after new deals with Apple, Huawei and Transsion.

Investment management company First Pacific Advisors recently released its "FPA Queens Road Value Fund" Q3 2026 investor letter. A copy of the letter can be downloaded here. The Fund returned -1.82% in the third quarter of 2026, underperforming the S&P 500 Value Index, which gained 0.90%, while its year-to-date return reached 9.16%, slightly ahead of the benchmark's 9.01%. Higher financing costs and conflict in the Middle East remained important influences on markets, creating an uneven environment in which strength in energy and health care offset weakness across industrials, utilities, and consumer-related businesses. The Fund's health care holdings provided the strongest support, while financial positions remained relatively steady; however, gains in these areas were insufficient to offset a pullback in technology holdings following their strong first-half performance. The Fund's lack of energy exposure also weighed on relative returns as oil prices rose more than 30%, and its average cash position was 8% during the quarter. Looking ahead, the firm expects higher interest rates and energy prices to continue testing businesses and investment portfolios. Its approach remains focused on companies with strong balance sheets, capable management teams, durable competitive positions, and reasonable valuations, which the managers believe are essential qualities for generating attractive returns over a full investment cycle. In addition, please check the Fund's top five holdings to know its best picks in 2026.

In its third-quarter 2026 investor letter, FPA Queens Road Value Fund highlighted stocks like Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC). Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC) is a semiconductor manufacturer that designs and produces processors, chips, and other computing components used in personal computers, servers, data centers, and other technology products. The one-month return of Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC) was -39.13% while its shares traded between $52.63 and $56.48 over the last 52 weeks. On November 19th, 2026, Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC) stock closed at approximately $55.72 per share, with a market capitalization of about $296.15 billion.

FPA Queens Road Value Fund stated the following regarding Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC) in its Q3 2026 investor letter:

"Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC) declined about 14% for the quarter, giving back a portion of the sharp gains it made through the spring and early summer. In August, the company sold $20 billion of new stock at $95 per share to fund a capital spending program that now exceeds $20 billion in 2026. CEO Lip-Bu Tan personally purchased roughly $10 million of shares at the same price. Management says demand for server processors far outpaces supply; the question for investors is how much capital it will take to meet it. Semiconductors have long been a cyclical business, and periods of tight supply have often encouraged the industry to build more capacity than demand ultimately required. Artificial intelligence may prove to be a more durable source of demand than past cycles, but the cost of participating keeps rising, and we expect the market to remain sensitive to any sign that spending is getting ahead of returns."
